title: Green Thumb Landscaping: year-end payroll reporting
participant_role: Payroll accountant at an accounting firm
judge_role: Owner of GREEN THUMB LANDSCAPING, a seasonal business closing out its payroll for the year

difficulty.rationale: Year-end employer payroll taxes with wage bases, plus filing deadlines.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of a payroll accountant at an accounting firm. The owner (judge) of GREEN THUMB LANDSCAPING, a client, has asked you to help close out the company's payroll for the year.

GREEN THUMB LANDSCAPING mows lawns, plants gardens and removes snow for homes and small businesses. The company has two full-time employees who work all year and hires extra seasonal workers each summer. This year two seasonal workers, Chloe and Dev, worked from May through August and then returned to school.

The owner (judge) has always paid employees on time but has never paid close attention to what payroll really costs beyond wages. Now that the year is ending, the owner (judge) has received several reminders about year-end forms and is not sure what must be filed, when it is due or who must receive copies. The owner (judge) keeps paper timecards in a folder in the truck and is not sure which records must be kept or for how long.

The owner (judge) also plans to hire more seasonal workers next spring and has heard that each state has its own payroll rules. The owner (judge) wants to be sure the company is following them.

[Annual wages: see exhibits]

[Employer payroll tax and insurance rates: see exhibits]

You must:
- Explain the types of payroll expenses an employer pays
- Calculate this year's employer payroll taxes and workers' compensation insurance
- List the year-end payroll returns and reports and their deadlines
- Explain what employee earnings records the business must keep
- Explain the state requirements the business must meet

You will present your information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's office at the company's garage. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Chloe and Dev only worked summer. Do they still get W-2s?
Can I skip workers' comp since we've never had an injury?

solution.overview: A strong answer explains each type of payroll expense, applies the correct wage bases to compute employer FICA of $6,349.50, FUTA of $150, SUTA of $930 and workers' compensation of $3,320 (total $10,749.50), and lists the year-end filings (W-2, W-3, fourth-quarter 941 and 940, all due January 31, plus state reports). The presenter then explains what earnings records to keep and the state rules the business must follow.

answer: Gross wages paid to employees
Employer share of Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%), matching what employees pay
FUTA and SUTA unemployment taxes, paid only by the employer and only up to each wage base
Workers' compensation insurance, which covers employees injured on the job
Withholdings (income tax, the employee's FICA) are not an employer expense; the business only holds and remits them
Total employer cost beyond wages = $10,749.50
Form W-2 to each employee, including Chloe and Dev, by January 31
Form W-3 with copies of all W-2s to the Social Security Administration by January 31
Fourth-quarter Form 941 (withholding and FICA) by January 31
Form 940 (annual FUTA return) by January 31
State withholding and unemployment reports on the state's schedule
Timecards or time sheets showing hours worked each day
An employee earnings record for each person: hours, gross pay, deductions, net pay and year-to-date totals
Form W-4 for withholding and Form I-9 for work eligibility
Keep payroll tax records at least 4 years, stored safely (not in the truck) with limited access
Register with the state for withholding and unemployment tax accounts
Report each new hire to the state, including seasonal workers
Carry workers' compensation coverage as required by state law
Follow the state's minimum wage and final paycheck rules

calculations.label: Total employer payroll taxes and insurance

judge_question_answers.question: Chloe and Dev only worked summer. Do they still get W-2s?
answer: Yes: every employee who was paid wages during the year gets a Form W-2, no matter how short the job
Mail them to their current addresses by January 31
Their wages are also included on Form W-3, Form 941 and the state reports
Keep their earnings records like everyone else's

judge_question_answers.question: Can I skip workers' comp since we've never had an injury?
answer: No: state law requires workers' compensation coverage for employees
Landscaping uses mowers, trimmers and trucks, so the chance of injury is real
Without coverage, the owner could personally pay medical bills and lost wages, plus state fines or stop-work orders
The $3,320 premium is a small cost compared with one serious injury

key_concepts.definition: The employer's total cost of employees: gross wages plus employer payroll taxes and insurance such as workers' compensation.
The employer's matching share of Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%), 7.65% in total, paid on top of wages.
Federal unemployment tax paid only by the employer, at an effective 0.6% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages.
State unemployment tax paid by the employer on each employee's wages up to the state's wage base; the rate and base vary by state.
The maximum amount of each employee's yearly wages that a tax applies to. Wages above the base are not taxed.
State-required insurance that pays medical costs and lost wages for employees injured on the job; premiums are based on wages and job risk.
A record for each employee showing hours, gross pay, each deduction, net pay and year-to-date totals; used to prepare W-2s and payroll returns.
The W-2 reports one employee's yearly wages and withholding; the W-3 summarizes all W-2s for the Social Security Administration. Both are due January 31.
Form 941 is the quarterly federal return for withholding and FICA; Form 940 is the annual FUTA return.
A state requirement to report newly hired employees, which helps enforce child support orders.

notes: State level because students must apply different wage bases to each employee and explain the full year-end filing calendar. Common mistakes: charging FUTA or SUTA on all wages instead of only up to each wage base, and forgetting that seasonal workers also need W-2s.

items.label: Explain the nature of payroll expenses

criteria.exceeds: Explains gross wages, the employer's matching Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%), employer-only FUTA and SUTA up to each wage base, and workers' compensation, and makes clear that withholdings are held and remitted, not an employer expense, so the true cost beyond wages is $10,749.50.
criteria.meets: Identifies wages, employer FICA, FUTA, SUTA and workers' compensation as employer payroll expenses and separates them from employee withholdings.
criteria.below: Lists only some expenses, or counts employee withholdings as a cost to the employer.
criteria.little: Does not explain payroll expenses beyond wages.

criteria.exceeds: Lists timecards, an employee earnings record for each person (hours, gross pay, deductions, net pay and year-to-date totals), Forms W-4 and I-9, and says to keep payroll tax records at least 4 years in a safe place with limited access instead of a folder in the truck, including records for Chloe and Dev.
criteria.meets: Identifies timecards, individual earnings records and W-4 and I-9 forms and states the at least 4 year retention period.
criteria.below: Mentions keeping records in general without naming what is required or how long to keep them.
criteria.little: Does not address earnings records, or accepts keeping timecards in the truck.

items.label: Prepare federal, state, and local payroll tax returns and reports

criteria.exceeds: Lists Form W-2 to every employee including Chloe and Dev, Form W-3 with W-2 copies to the Social Security Administration, the fourth-quarter Form 941 and the annual Form 940, all due January 31, plus state withholding and unemployment reports on the state's schedule, and explains what each reports.
criteria.meets: Names the W-2, W-3, Form 941 and Form 940 with the January 31 deadline and mentions state reports.
criteria.below: Names only some of the forms, gives wrong deadlines, or leaves the seasonal workers off the W-2s.
criteria.little: Cannot identify the year-end returns and reports.

criteria.exceeds: Explains registering for state withholding and unemployment accounts, reporting every new hire including next spring's seasonal workers, carrying required workers' compensation, following state minimum wage and final paycheck rules, and applying the state's own $10,000 SUTA wage base.
criteria.meets: Identifies state registration, new hire reporting, required workers' compensation and minimum wage rules.
criteria.below: Mentions that states have rules without naming specific requirements.

criteria.exceeds: Calculates employer FICA $6,349.50 (83,000 x 7.65%), FUTA $150 on $25,000 of taxable wages, SUTA $930 on $31,000 of taxable wages and workers' compensation $3,320 ($4 per $100), a total of $10,749.50, and explains that withheld and employer taxes are remitted with the returns.
criteria.meets: Calculates FICA $6,349.50, FUTA $150, SUTA $930 and workers' compensation $3,320 for a total of $10,749.50.
criteria.below: Gets some amounts right but applies FUTA or SUTA to all $83,000 of wages (for example FUTA $498 or SUTA $2,490), or leaves out an item.
criteria.little: Does not calculate the employer payroll taxes, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibit.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Applies each wage base to each employee (Chloe and Dev below both limits, Ana and Ben capped) and connects the taxes, records, returns and state rules into one year-end process.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibits to the taxable wages and total employer cost.
criteria.below: Reaches some answers without showing the reasoning, or misses how the wage bases work.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives the owner a practical plan: a January 31 filing checklist, secure record storage, state registration and new hire reporting before next spring, and budgeting about $10,749.50 beyond wages.
criteria.meets: Gives clear steps the owner should take to finish year-end payroll correctly.
criteria.below: Gives advice that is partly correct or not clearly stated.

criteria.exceeds: Explains taxes, wage bases and forms in plain language the owner can follow, in a logical order, with confident and professional delivery.
criteria.meets: Presents the expenses, calculations, filings, records and state rules clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on form numbers without explanation, or skips topics.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a table of taxable wages by employee or a year-end calendar of forms and deadlines, and adds a useful idea such as moving to payroll software or digital timecards.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes it easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: yes, every employee paid wages gets a W-2 by January 31, mailed to current addresses and included on the W-3, Form 941 and state reports; and no, state law requires workers' compensation, landscaping equipment makes injury a real risk, and without coverage the owner could pay medical bills and lost wages plus fines, which the $3,320 premium avoids.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that seasonal workers get W-2s and that workers' compensation is required by state law.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without the deadline or the legal requirement.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says the seasonal workers need no W-2 or that workers' compensation can be skipped.

key_points: Employer FICA: 83,000 x 7.65% = $6,349.50 ($5,146.00 Social Security plus $1,203.50 Medicare)
Workers' compensation: 83,000 / 100 x $4 = $3,320; total employer cost beyond wages $10,749.50
Withholdings are held and remitted for employees, not an employer expense
W-2s to every employee (including Chloe and Dev), W-3, fourth-quarter Form 941 and Form 940 are all due January 31, plus state reports
Keep timecards, earnings records, W-4s and I-9s; payroll tax records at least 4 years, stored securely
State rules: register for withholding and unemployment accounts, report new hires, carry workers' compensation, follow minimum wage and final paycheck rules
